metadata.title: Planck vs Rayleigh-Jeans — Linear Scale Hides the Catastrophe
metadata.purpose: viz-riff critique of vol1-planck-vs-rj.html — judges the visualization, not the physics

beats.narration_text: Ciao, Liam. I'm Liam, in for Bear. Someone asked Claude to build a visualization of the Planck versus Rayleigh-Jeans blackbody spectrum — the UV catastrophe. Claude returned a two-panel D3 simulation. Today we judge the visualization, not the physics.

props.command: write me a visualization of the Planck vs Rayleigh-Jeans blackbody spectrum
props.runningText: Hey Claude, write me a visualization for the Planck vs Rayleigh-Jeans blackbody spectrum.

beats.narration_text: Two panels. Left: spectral energy density, linear Y-axis in scientific notation. Planck curve solid ink. Rayleigh-Jeans dashed red. A gray dashed line marks the Wien peak. Right panel: the Planck-to-Rayleigh-Jeans ratio on a zero-to-one scale. One slider for temperature — one thousand to ten thousand Kelvin. One dropdown to switch the x-axis between frequency and wavelength. That is the full inventory.

Drag temperature from one thousand to ten thousand Kelvin. Both panels update. The Planck peak shifts right — Wien's law, peak frequency proportional to T. The x-axis auto-scales to keep that peak in frame at every temperature. Rayleigh-Jeans is always above Planck, always clipped at the top of the plot, always labeled RJ goes to infinity. The ratio panel barely changes shape — that is because x equals h-nu over k-B-T, and temperature cancels. The suppression is temperature-independent in shape.

Two things this visualization does correctly. First: the companion ratio panel. It isolates the quantum correction factor on a zero-to-one scale, so the suppression is a visible number, not a squinting contest between two curves. The readout says ten-to-the-minus-twenty at UV — that magnitude is in the display, not buried in a footnote. Second: the domain auto-scales with temperature in frequency mode. The Wien peak is always on screen, at every temperature from one thousand to ten thousand Kelvin. A fixed domain would lose the peak off the right edge at high temperature.

The main panel uses a linear Y-axis. That forces Rayleigh-Jeans to be clipped at just over the Planck peak. On screen, the two curves look almost identical — only the clip edge and the RJ-goes-to-infinity label reveal the divergence. The ten-to-the-minus-twenty magnitude is in the readout text, not in the visual shape. A log Y-axis would make both curves simultaneously visible, with Rayleigh-Jeans shooting upward with the correct visual weight. The ratio panel is also linear — the exponential suppression curve immediately hugs the bottom, and the structure of how fast it falls is invisible. Finally: switching the x-axis from frequency to wavelength applies a Jacobian coordinate change with no explanation. A student will believe the physics changed.

Let's recap with Claude. The two-panel design is the right call — the ratio panel is where the argument lives. But the linear Y-axis on the main panel makes the ultraviolet catastrophe look like a mild discrepancy. The ten-to-the-minus-twenty is in the readout, not in the image. A log Y-axis changes that. Best used after deriving the Planck formula, not as the introduction to the catastrophe.

artifactLines: Two-panel design: ratio panel isolates the quantum correction factor
Linear Y-axis clips Rayleigh-Jeans — catastrophe magnitude is in text, not image
Ratio panel also linear: exponential suppression structure disappears
Use after deriving Planck — not as the introduction to the catastrophe

beats.narration_text: Take this Planck versus Rayleigh-Jeans simulation and make one change: replace the linear Y-axis on the spectral energy density panel with a logarithmic scale. Keep both curves on the same plot so the Rayleigh-Jeans divergence is visible rather than clipped. Then add a one-line note below the ratio panel explaining that Planck-over-RJ is the Bose-Einstein quantum correction factor, x divided by open-paren e-to-the-x minus one close-paren, where x equals h-nu over k-B-T. Finally, add a second annotation: at what temperature does the ratio drop below one-half at visible-light frequencies?

props.command: Take this Planck vs Rayleigh-Jeans simulation and make one change: replace the linear Y-axis with a log scale. Keep both curves on the same plot. Then add a note below the ratio panel: Planck/RJ is the Bose-Einstein factor x/(e^x − 1), x = hν/kBT. Finally: at what temperature does the ratio drop below 0.5 at visible-light frequencies?
